summary: This document defines metadata for delegating HTTPS content delivery among interconnected CDNs. It adds a CDNI Metadata interface object for delegating X.509 certificates, using the schemes of RFC 9115. The delegating party stays in full control and can revoke at any time, with no need to share private keys.

eli5.summary: You let a friend's shop sell for you, giving them a limited pass rather than your own house key. You can take the pass back anytime.

questions: cdn certificate delegation without sharing keys
how does a cdn get a certificate for another cdn
subtitle: How one CDN tells another it may get HTTPS certificates for a customer's domain without ever handing over private keys.

tldr.problem: When one CDN hands traffic to another CDN using DNS redirection, the second CDN must present a certificate for the content provider's domain name, but sharing private keys between CDNs is risky.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9538 defines a CDNI metadata object, ACMEDelegationMethod, that points the downstream CDN at an ACME delegation resource on the upstream CDN and carries the validity window and, for short-term certificates, the lifetime settings.
tldr.outcome: The downstream CDN can obtain a certificate for the delegated name with its own key pair, and the delegating side stays in control and can revoke the delegation at any time.

today: RFC 9538 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2024, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It depends on the ACME delegation profile in RFC 9115.

sections.title: The Problem: HTTPS Across Several CDNs
sections.content:
When content is delivered over HTTPS by two or more cooperating CDNs, credentials have to be managed. This matters most when DNS-based redirection is used: the upstream CDN (uCDN) sends the user to a downstream CDN (dCDN), and the dCDN must prove to the end user that it speaks for the content provider's domain.

RFC 9538 builds on RFC 9115, which defines delegation methods where a uCDN, acting for the content provider that holds the domain, can generate on demand an X.509 certificate binding the domain name to a key pair owned by the dCDN. RFC 9538 adds the CDNI metadata needed to use that mechanism, and registers a new payload type in the "CDNI Payload Types" IANA registry.
sections.eli5: A big store lets a partner store sell its products. The partner needs a badge that says it is allowed to do so. This document explains how the badge gets requested.

sections.title: Advertising Support Through FCI
sections.content:
The Footprint and Capabilities Advertisement interface (FCI) from RFC 8008 lets a dCDN tell a uCDN what it can do. RFC 9538 reuses the capability serialization from that RFC to let a dCDN say which delegation methods it supports.

The example in the RFC uses a capability of type FCI.Metadata whose value lists ACMEDelegationMethod in its metadata array, next to the usual footprint objects.
sections.eli5: Before a partner can be given a badge, it first says, "I know how to use badges of this kind."

sections.title: How ACME Delegation Fits Into CDNI
sections.content:
When a uCDN delegates HTTPS delivery to a dCDN through DNS redirection, the dCDN must use a certificate bound to the origin's name to authenticate to the end user. The new object describes metadata for using the ACME delegation interface of RFC 9115.

It covers two cases. STAR delegation uses short-term, automatically renewed certificates (RFC 8739). Non-STAR delegation lets CDNs delegate with long-term certificates.

The RFC's Figure 1 shows the STAR flow. The dCDN fetches metadata from the uCDN over CDNI and receives the delegation configuration. It fetches the delegation over ACME and gets a CSR template. It creates a key pair and a certificate signing request with the delegated name, and posts an order to the uCDN. The uCDN forwards the order to the Certification Authority (CA) as an ACME STAR order. After authorizations and issuance, the dCDN fetches the certificate from the CA without authentication.

The delegation object in RFC 9115 only allows DNS mappings through CNAME records. The RFC notes that a future document could extend it to SVCB/HTTPS-based mappings (RFC 9460).
sections.eli5: The partner makes its own secret stamp, asks the big store to vouch for it, and the big store asks the official office to print a badge. The partner never sees the store's own keys.

sections.title: The ACMEDelegationMethod Object
sections.content:
The object lets a uCDN define both STAR and non-STAR delegations. The dCDN tells them apart by the presence of the lifetime property: if it is there, the delegation is short-term; if it is absent, it is a non-STAR delegation.

  • acme-delegation (string, mandatory): a URL of an ACME delegation object tied to the dCDN's account on the uCDN's ACME server. It MUST use the https scheme.
  • time-window (TimeWindow, mandatory): the validity period, using the RFC 8006 TimeWindow with start and end. For STAR these are the start-date and end-date of the certificate validity; for non-STAR they are the notBefore and notAfter fields of the certificate.
  • lifetime (integer): mandatory only for a STAR delegation, as defined in RFC 8739.
  • lifetime-adjust (integer, optional): as defined in RFC 8739.
sections.eli5: It is a small form with a few boxes: where to ask, from when to when the badge works, and, for badges that renew themselves, how long each one lasts.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives two examples, both with generic-metadata-type set to MI.ACMEDelegationMethod. The STAR example has an acme-delegation URL on acme.ucdn.example, a time window from 1665417434 to 1665676634, a lifetime of 345600 and a lifetime-adjust of 259200.

The non-STAR example has only the URL and a time window from 1570982234 to 1665417434, with no lifetime property.
sections.eli5: One sample form is for a badge that renews itself, and one is for a badge that lasts for a single long stretch.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the new object adds no security or privacy concerns beyond those in RFC 9115, RFC 8006 and RFC 8008. Readers are expected to understand the ACME delegation trust model and security goal in RFC 9115.

The dCDN's ACME account is critical: it authorizes all security-relevant operations between the dCDN and the uCDN over ACME. The acme-delegation resource is only reachable by the account key holder, who may fetch it only by POST-as-GET. The Metadata interface authentication and confidentiality requirements of RFC 8006 MUST be followed, implementers MUST follow the security considerations of RFC 8008, and where TLS is used the guidance in RFC 9325 MUST be followed.
sections.eli5: The account is like the master key to the badge office, so it must be guarded well. Only its owner can look at the paperwork.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC registers one payload type, MI.ACMEDelegationMethod, in the "CDNI Payload Types" registry. Its purpose is to distinguish ACMEDelegationMethod Metadata Interface objects and any associated capability advertisement. It applies to the MI/FCI interfaces and is encoded as described in the object definition.
sections.eli5: The new kind of form gets its name written in the official list so everyone uses the same label.
